overview.h1: HTS Chapter 09: Coffee, tea, maté and spices — Tariff Rates

seo.title: HTS Chapter 09: Coffee, Tea, Maté & Spices — Tariff Rates & Import Duties | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: Searchable U.S. duty table for all 91 HTS Chapter 09 lines — green and roasted coffee, tea, maté, pepper, vanilla, cinnamon, cumin, ginger and other spices — with General, FTA and Column 2 rates and the 2026 Section 301 exemption for coffee, tea and spices.

overview.intro:
Chapter 09 covers coffee (green, roasted and decaffeinated), tea, maté and the dried spices: pepper, chilies and paprika, vanilla, cinnamon, cloves, nutmeg and cardamom, cumin and other seeds, ginger, turmeric, saffron, thyme and spice mixtures. Its **91 tariff lines** are almost all **Free** at the base rate. Only 19 carry a duty, all small: 6.4% on flavored green tea, 1.9%–4.8% on spice mixtures, thyme, bay leaves and origanum, and 1¢–7.4¢/kg on ground ginger, dried capsicum and Bombay mace.

The extra duties by country mostly skip this chapter. Since **July 24, 2026** the Section 301 tariff on 60 economies (10% or 12.5%) and Brazil's 25% Section 301 tariff both exempt **every Chapter 09 line except crude thyme and bay leaves (0910.99.05) and thyme (0910.99.06)** (U.S. notes 52(b) and 50(a)(ii) to Chapter 99). So green coffee from Brazil, Colombia or Vietnam enters free. The one broad extra duty is China's **+7.5%** Section 301 List 4A, which covers every line. The 2025 IEEPA tariffs, which had put 50% on Brazilian coffee from August 6 to November 12, 2025, ended on February 24, 2026. The U.S. imported **$15.51B** of Chapter 09 goods in 2025, 83% of it coffee.

productGroups.label: Coffee, whether or not roasted or decaffeinated
productGroups.blurb: Green, roasted and decaffeinated coffee is Free from every country except China (+7.5%). Coffee lines are split by arabica, robusta and certified organic since July 1, 2025. Only coffee substitutes containing coffee carry a duty (1.5¢/kg).

productGroups.label: Tea, whether or not flavored
productGroups.blurb: Plain green and black tea are Free. Flavored green tea pays 6.4% (Free with most FTAs, 3.2% for Japan). Lines are split by packing size (3 kg) and organic status.

productGroups.label: Maté
productGroups.blurb: Maté (yerba mate) is Free from every country except China (+7.5%).

productGroups.label: Pepper of the genus Piper
productGroups.blurb: Black and white peppercorns, whole or ground, are Free. Dried capsicum (paprika, cayenne, ancho, chili) pays 2.5¢–5¢/kg unless an FTA applies; allspice is Free.

productGroups.label: Vanilla
productGroups.blurb: Vanilla beans and ground vanilla are Free.

productGroups.label: Cinnamon and cinnamon-tree flowers
productGroups.blurb: Cinnamon and cassia, whole or ground, are Free.

productGroups.label: Cloves (whole fruit, cloves and stems)
productGroups.blurb: Cloves, whole or ground, are Free.

productGroups.label: Nutmeg, mace and cardamoms
productGroups.blurb: Nutmeg, mace and cardamom are Free, except ground Bombay or wild mace at 7.4¢/kg.

productGroups.label: Seeds of anise, badian, fennel, coriander, cumin or caraway
productGroups.blurb: Coriander, cumin, anise, star anise, caraway and fennel seeds and juniper berries are Free.

productGroups.label: Ginger, saffron, turmeric (curcuma), thyme, bay leaves…
productGroups.blurb: Ginger, saffron, turmeric and curry are Free (ground ginger 1¢/kg). Spice mixtures pay 1.9%, manufactured thyme 4.8%, bay leaves 3.2% and origanum 3.4%. The two thyme and bay-leaf lines 0910.99.05 and 0910.99.06 are the only Chapter 09 lines that pay the 2026 Section 301 duty.

workedExamples.title: A container of green arabica coffee from Brazil
workedExamples.body: Green coffee is Free at the base rate. Brazil's 25% Section 301 duty (9903.05.01) and the 12.5% forced-labor Section 301 duty (9903.05.27) both exempt it (9903.05.03, 9903.05.86), so a $150,000 container pays **$0** in duty. Between August 6 and November 12, 2025 the same container paid 10% reciprocal plus 40% Brazil IEEPA duty: **$75,000**.

workedExamples.title: Flavored green tea from Japan
workedExamples.body: The general rate is 6.4%, but Japan's agreement rate is **3.2%** (SPI JP). Japan's 12.5% Section 301 rate does not apply because the line is on the U.S. note 52(b) exemption list. A $20,000 shipment pays $640 with the JP claim, or $1,280 without it. Plain (unflavored) green tea and matcha in 0902.10.90 are Free.

workedExamples.title: Dried thyme from India
workedExamples.body: Manufactured thyme is 4.8%, and it is one of the two Chapter 09 lines not exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty, so India's +10% (9903.05.44) applies: **14.8%**, or $1,480 on a $10,000 shipment. Crude thyme (0910.99.05) has a Free base rate but still pays the 10%.

workedExamples.title: Ground cinnamon from China
workedExamples.body: Free at the base rate and exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty, but China's Section 301 List 4A adds **7.5%** (9903.88.15): $750 on a $10,000 shipment. Ground cinnamon is also on FDA Import Alert 99-42 for lead, so shipments from listed firms are detained.

**Note 1.** Mixtures of the products of headings 0904 to 0910 are classified as follows: (a) mixtures of two or more products of the same heading go in that heading; (b) mixtures of products of different headings go in heading 0910. seo.shortDescription: What changed for U.S. coffee, tea and spice tariffs since January 2025: the 50% Brazil coffee tariff and its removal, the November 2025 agricultural exemption, the end of IEEPA tariffs, and the 2026 Section 301 exemption, with Federal Register citations.

tariffUpdates.intro:
This page compares two editions of the tariff schedule: the **2025 Basic Edition**, in force at the start of 2025, and the current **2026 Revision 21** (in force October 9, 2026). No Chapter 09 base rate changed. The only line changes are statistical: on July 1, 2025 the coffee lines were split by arabica, robusta and other, which renumbered 24 lines. All of them are Free.

The big changes were extra duties by country. In 2025 coffee, tea and spices paid the IEEPA reciprocal tariff, and Brazilian coffee paid **50%** from August 6. On **November 13, 2025** coffee, tea and spices were exempted from the reciprocal tariff for every country and from Brazil's 40% duty. All IEEPA tariffs **ended on February 24, 2026**. The 10% Section 122 surcharge that followed and the 2026 Section 301 tariffs both exempt every Chapter 09 line except two thyme and bay-leaf lines (0910.99.05 and 0910.99.06). Today the only broad extra duty is **China's +7.5%** (Section 301 List 4A).

For the rate each supplier pays, see Rates by country.

changes.title: No Chapter 09 base-rate changes
changes.detail: Every Chapter 09 line that exists in both editions carries the same General rate in the 2026 Revision 21 as in the 2025 Basic Edition. The 24 new statistical lines are the coffee lines renumbered on July 1, 2025; all are Free.

changes.title: China Section 301 List 4A continues
changes.detail: USTR announced that the China Section 301 actions continue during the four-year review. For Chapter 09 this keeps +7.5% (9903.88.15) on every line from China.

changes.title: Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies; coffee, tea and spices exempt
changes.detail: 10% or 12.5% on all products of 60 economies (9903.05.20–9903.05.84), including Brazil, Colombia, Vietnam, India, Indonesia, Peru and the Central American coffee producers. U.S. note 52(b) (9903.05.86) exempts every Chapter 09 line except 0910.99.05 (crude thyme and bay leaves) and 0910.99.06 (thyme). USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico are exempt (9903.05.93, 9903.05.94).

changes.title: Section 122 import surcharge expired
changes.detail: The 150-day surcharge (9903.03.01) expired at the close of July 23, 2026.

changes.title: 25% Section 301 tariff on Brazil; coffee, tea and spices exempt
changes.detail: USTR imposed 25% on all products of Brazil (9903.05.01). U.S. note 50(a)(ii) (9903.05.03) exempts every Chapter 09 line except 0910.99.05 and 0910.99.06, so Brazilian coffee, pepper and maté stay free. From July 24 those two lines also pay Brazil's 12.5% under 9903.05.27.

changes.title: USMCA joint review: not renewed, still in force
changes.detail: The United States did not agree to renew the USMCA in its current form. USTR said the Agreement remains in force pending resolution of the issues or until termination, so USMCA claims (SPI S) still apply.

changes.title: Section 122 surcharge replaces the IEEPA tariffs; coffee, tea and spices exempt
changes.detail: 10% on products of all countries (9903.03.01) until July 23, 2026. Its product exemption list (9903.03.03) carried over the agricultural exemption, covering every Chapter 09 line except 0910.99.05 and 0910.99.06. USMCA-qualifying goods from Canada and Mexico were exempt (9903.03.07, 9903.03.08).

changes.title: All IEEPA tariffs end
changes.detail: After the Supreme Court held on February 20, 2026 (Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump) that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs, Executive Order 14389 ended the Canada, Mexico, China, Brazil and reciprocal duties, and CBP stopped collecting them for goods entered from 12:00 a.m. ET on February 24. The 9903.01.xx and 9903.02.xx headings are still printed in Revision 21 but are no longer in effect.

changes.title: Additional 25% duty on products of India ended
changes.detail: Executive Order 14384 ended the additional 25% duty on products of India (9903.01.84) that had applied since August 27, 2025.

changes.title: AGOA reauthorized through December 31, 2026
changes.detail: AGOA was renewed retroactively from September 30, 2025, when it had lapsed. AGOA (SPI D) makes the dutiable spice and flavored-tea lines Free for eligible sub-Saharan countries. GSP (SPI A, A+, A*) remains expired since December 31, 2020.

changes.title: Nicaragua Section 301 duty scheduled for 2027 and 2028
changes.detail: USTR set a duty on products of Nicaragua under 9903.89.01: 0% in 2026, +10% from January 1, 2027 and +15% from January 1, 2028. It reaches every Chapter 09 line (the note 52(b) exemption does not cover it) but applies only to goods not entered under CAFTA-DR, so Nicaraguan coffee claimed under CAFTA-DR (SPI P) stays free.

changes.title: Coffee, tea and spices exempted from the reciprocal tariff
changes.detail: Executive Order 14360 (signed November 14, 2025, effective for goods entered from November 13) added coffee, tea, maté and spices to the reciprocal-tariff exemption list in U.S. note 2(v)(iii) — every Chapter 09 line except 0910.99.05 and 0910.99.06 — for all countries. Duties paid from November 13 were refundable.
changes.countries: All countries subject to the reciprocal tariff

changes.title: Brazil's 40% duty lifted from coffee and other farm goods
changes.detail: Executive Order 14361 (signed November 20, 2025) took coffee, tea, maté and spices off Brazil's 40% IEEPA duty (9903.01.77) for goods entered from November 13, 2025. With EO 14360 removing the 10% reciprocal duty, Brazilian green coffee went from 50% to Free.

changes.title: China fentanyl duty cut to 10%
changes.detail: The IEEPA duty on products of China and Hong Kong (9903.01.24) fell from +20% to +10%. Unlike the reciprocal tariff, it had no agricultural exemption, so it applied to Chinese ginger, tea and spices until it ended on February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Additional 25% duty on products of India
changes.detail: Executive Order 14329 added 25% (9903.01.84) on products of India on top of the 25% reciprocal rate. Ended February 7, 2026.

changes.title: Country-specific reciprocal rates
changes.detail: Executive Order 14326 replaced the 10% baseline with country rates for listed countries, for example Vietnam +20% (9903.02.69), Indonesia +19% (9903.02.27) and India +25% (9903.02.26). Coffee, tea and spices were not exempt until November 13, 2025. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: 40% duty on products of Brazil, coffee included
changes.detail: Executive Order 14323 (signed July 30, 2025) added 40% on products of Brazil (9903.01.77) on top of the 10% reciprocal duty. Its exemption list did not include coffee, so Brazilian green coffee paid 50% until November 13, 2025. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Coffee statistical lines split by arabica, robusta and other
changes.detail: HTS 2025 Revision 16 discontinued the old 0901.11–0901.22 statistical suffixes and set up new ones for arabica, robusta and other coffee, each with a certified-organic line. Rates did not change; all are Free.

changes.title: Reciprocal tariff reaches coffee, tea and spices
changes.detail: 10% baseline on products of all countries (9903.01.25), with no exemption for Chapter 09 at first; Canada and Mexico were excluded. Coffee, tea and spices were exempted on November 13, 2025, and the tariff ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: China fentanyl duty raised to 20%
changes.detail: The IEEPA duty on products of China and Hong Kong (9903.01.20, then 9903.01.24) went from +10% (from February 4, 2025) to +20%, on top of the 7.5% List 4A duty.

changes.title: Additional duties on products of Canada and Mexico
changes.detail: +25% on non-USMCA goods of Canada (9903.01.10, raised to +35% from August 1, 2025) and Mexico (9903.01.01); USMCA-qualifying goods exempt. Ended February 24, 2026.

understandIndustry.why:
U.S. imports of Chapter 09 goods rose from **$11.70B in 2024 to $15.51B in 2025** (+32.5%). Coffee (heading 0901) explains almost all of it: $8.99B to $12.80B, and green coffee alone (0901.11) rose 55.5% to $9.83B. Comtrade values measure dollars, not tonnes, so the rise mixes higher coffee prices with volume.

The supplier mix moved too. Imports from **Colombia** rose 81.5% to $2.76B and passed **Brazil** ($2.56B, +24.4%). From August 6 to November 12, 2025 Brazilian coffee paid a 50% IEEPA duty, while Colombian coffee paid 10% and, like all coffee, nothing from November 13. Honduras (+75.2%), Mexico (+56.6%) and Peru (+54.5%) also grew fast; imports from Canada fell 16.2%.

Outside coffee the chapter is spread thin: pepper and capsicum $1.15B (Vietnam 39%), tea $620M (Japan 31%), ginger, turmeric and other 0910 spices $458M (India, China, Peru), cinnamon $169M (Indonesia, Vietnam, Sri Lanka) and vanilla $101M (Madagascar 70%). 2025 is the latest full year of U.S. trade data.

industryAreas.intro:
For Chapter 09 the country matters much less than for most chapters. Each cell below is the base rate for that product group plus the extra duty for that country, minus any preference, from the current tariff schedule.

The 2026 Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies and on Brazil exempt **every Chapter 09 line except crude thyme and bay leaves (0910.99.05) and thyme (0910.99.06)**, so **coffee, tea, maté and nearly all spices pay only their base rate** — Free for most lines — from Brazil, Colombia, Vietnam, Switzerland or anywhere else. The exception is **China**, where Section 301 List 4A adds **7.5%** to every line. The extra duties show up only in the 0910 column, on those two thyme and bay-leaf lines.

tariffEngineering.h1: HTS Chapter 09: Coffee, tea, maté and spices — Import Documents & Ways to Lower Duty

seo.title: Importing Coffee, Tea & Spices: FDA Rules, Documents & Legal Ways to Lower Duty (HTS Ch. 09) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: The FDA, USDA and CBP rules for each HTS Chapter 09 line — prior notice, FSVP, spice import alerts, organic certificates, APHIS coffee and khapra rules — and the legal ways to pay less: the Section 301 exemption, FTA and AGOA claims, drawback.
keywords: how to import coffee beans to usa
do you need a license to import coffee

tariffEngineering.intro:
Coffee, tea and spices are food, so **FDA rules decide whether a shipment is released**: prior notice before arrival, a registered foreign facility, a Foreign Supplier Verification Program, and import alerts that detain spices from listed firms for Salmonella or lead. USDA adds a few plant-health rules, and organic goods need an NOP Import Certificate. No import license is needed for coffee, tea or spices.

Most lines are already Free, so the ways to pay less are narrow: make sure the **Section 301 exemption** (9903.05.86) is reported, claim an FTA, USMCA or AGOA on the 19 dutiable lines, and choose the form (whole or crude) that carries the lower rate where that is an option.

levers.title: Report the Section 301 exemption heading for coffee, tea and spices
levers.saves: The 2026 Section 301 duty of 10% or 12.5% of value (and Brazil's separate 25%) on every Chapter 09 line except crude thyme and bay leaves (0910.99.05) and manufactured thyme (0910.99.06)
levers.appliesTo: 89 of 91 lines, from every country in the 60-economy action and from Brazil
levers.document: The entry lists the Chapter 99 exemption heading next to the Chapter 09 line: 9903.05.86 for the 60-economy duty (U.S. note 52(b)) and 9903.05.03 for the Brazil duty (U.S. note 50(a)(ii)).
levers.caveat: The exemption follows the 8-digit subheading, so the two thyme/bay-leaf lines above still pay. It does not lift the China List 4A duty (+7.5%, 9903.88.15) or the Nicaragua duty that starts on January 1, 2027 (9903.89.01).

levers.title: Claim a free trade agreement on the dutiable lines
levers.saves: The base rate on the 19 dutiable lines: 6.4% on flavored green tea, 1.9%–4.8% on spice mixtures, thyme, bay leaves and origanum, and 1¢–7.4¢/kg on ground ginger, dried capsicum and Bombay mace. Japan gets 3.2% instead of 6.4% on flavored green tea.
levers.appliesTo: Goods that originate in a partner country: Colombia (CO), Peru (PE), CAFTA-DR countries such as Guatemala, Honduras and Nicaragua (P), Australia, Chile, Korea, Singapore and the others listed in the line's Special column
levers.document: A certification of origin (or other information showing the goods originate) held by the importer when the claim is made, with the SPI code on the entry.
levers.caveat: Most Chapter 09 lines are already Free, so the claim only matters on the 19 dutiable lines. An FTA claim does not remove the Section 301 duty where it applies (U.S. note 52(a)). For Nicaragua it matters on every line from January 1, 2027: the new 9903.89.01 duty applies only to goods not entered under CAFTA-DR.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. notes 29 and 52(a)

levers.title: Claim USMCA on goods from Canada or Mexico
levers.saves: The base rate on the dutiable lines, and the 10% Section 301 duty on the two thyme/bay-leaf lines
levers.appliesTo: All 91 lines, for goods that qualify as originating under USMCA
levers.document: A certification of origin from the importer, exporter or producer, in the importer's possession when the claim is made. It need not follow a set format.
levers.caveat: Roasting or blending in Canada or Mexico does not by itself make coffee or tea grown elsewhere originating; check the product-specific rule. USMCA was not renewed at the July 1, 2026 joint review but remains in force.

citations.label: USTR statement on the USMCA joint review (July 1, 2026)

levers.title: Claim AGOA on spices and flavored tea from eligible African countries
levers.saves: The base rate on the dutiable lines that list SPI D (flavored green tea, spice mixtures, thyme, bay leaves, ground ginger, dried capsicum)
levers.appliesTo: Goods of AGOA beneficiary countries listed in HTSUS General Note 16
levers.document: The AGOA claim (SPI D) on the entry; the goods must be the growth, product or manufacture of the beneficiary country.
levers.caveat: AGOA was renewed only through December 31, 2026. GSP (SPI A, A+, A*) has been expired since December 31, 2020, so a GSP code in the Special column gives no benefit.

levers.title: Import in the form that carries the lower rate
levers.saves: Several spices are Free whole or crude but dutiable once processed: ginger is Free whole and 1¢/kg crushed or ground; thyme and bay leaves are Free crude (0910.99.05) but 4.8% and 3.2% once manufactured; origanum is Free crude and 3.4% otherwise; mace is Free except Bombay or wild mace, ground (7.4¢/kg).
levers.appliesTo: Ginger (0910.11 / 0910.12), thyme, bay leaves and origanum (0910.99), mace (0908.21 / 0908.22)
levers.document: Product specifications showing the condition of the goods as imported (whole, crude, crushed or ground).
levers.caveat: Classification follows the goods as they arrive, not how they will be used. Crude thyme and bay leaves (0910.99.05) still pay the Section 301 duty where it applies. A mixture of spices from different headings goes to 0910.91 (1.9%) under Chapter 09 note 1(b).

levers.title: Claim drawback on re-exported coffee, tea or spices
levers.saves: Up to 99% of the duties paid, including the Section 301 duty, when the goods (or products made from them) are exported
levers.appliesTo: Dutiable lines and any line that paid an extra duty, when the goods are exported or used to make exported goods
levers.document: A drawback claim filed with CBP, with import and export records that tie the goods together.
levers.caveat: Only worth it where a duty was actually paid; most Chapter 09 lines are Free with no extra duty.

levers.title: Get a binding ruling before you import
levers.saves: Certainty on lines where the classification decides the rate: flavored vs. plain tea, spice mixtures vs. seasonings (heading 2103), crude vs. manufactured herbs
levers.appliesTo: Any line where the classification decides the rate
levers.document: A ruling request to CBP describing the product, its ingredients and how it is packed.
levers.caveat: Rulings apply to the transaction described; a changed recipe may need its own ruling.

rules.title: Prior notice of imported food before arrival (2 hours by road, 4 by air or rail, 8 by water)
The foreign roaster, packer or warehouse must be registered as a food facility
Foreign Supplier Verification Program: the U.S. importer must verify each foreign supplier
Import Alert 99-19: spices from listed firms are detained without examination for Salmonella
Import Alerts 28-02 (black pepper from India: filth; each lot needs an Export Inspection Council certificate) and 28-04 (black and white pepper from Brazil: Salmonella)
Import Alert 99-42: ground cinnamon, turmeric and other foods from listed firms detained for lead and other heavy metals
Unroasted coffee, coffee leaves and used coffee sacks may not enter Hawaii or Puerto Rico (coffee berry borer and leaf rust); coffee seeds for planting need a plant permit
Fresh ginger root needs an APHIS fruit-and-vegetable permit; dried, cured or processed spices do not
Whole chilies, red peppers and cumin seed packed in new jute or burlap bags from khapra-beetle countries must be treated
Organic shipments must be certified, declared as organic to CBP and carry an NOP Import Certificate
Tea in packages under 2.3 kg: the packing is dutiable as if imported empty, unless the tea comes from a listed country (Chapter 09 additional U.S. note 4)
Pepper shells, ground or unground, may not be imported (Chapter 09 additional U.S. note 6)
Country-of-origin marking on the goods or their retail container

groups.label: Coffee, whether or not roasted or decaffeinated
groups.note: Coffee has no special FDA or APHIS permit on the mainland. Unroasted coffee cannot be shipped into Hawaii or Puerto Rico, and Puerto Rico may charge its own duty on coffee (Chapter 09 additional U.S. note 3).

groups.label: Tea, whether or not flavored
groups.note: The Tea Importation Act, which required FDA tea examiners, was repealed effective April 9, 1996; tea now follows the general food import rules.

groups.label: Pepper of the genus Piper
groups.note: Whole dried chilies and red peppers (0904.21) in new jute or burlap from khapra-beetle countries must be treated.

groups.label: Cinnamon and cinnamon-tree flowers
groups.note: Ground cinnamon is the main product on FDA's heavy-metals import alert after the 2024 lead findings.

groups.label: Seeds of anise, badian, fennel, coriander, cumin or caraway
groups.note: Cumin seed (0909.31) in new jute or burlap from khapra-beetle countries must be treated.

finalConclusion.intro: Straight answers to the most common questions about U.S. tariffs on coffee, tea and spices — by country, HS codes and import rules. Each answer links to the page with the full detail.
keyTakeaways: Coffee, tea, maté and almost all spices pay no extra U.S. tariff today: the 2026 Section 301 tariffs exempt every Chapter 09 line except two thyme and bay-leaf lines.
Brazilian coffee paid 50% from August 6 to November 12, 2025; since November 13, 2025 it has been free, and all IEEPA tariffs ended on February 24, 2026.
China is the exception: +7.5% (Section 301 List 4A) on every Chapter 09 line. From 2027, Nicaraguan goods not entered under CAFTA-DR pay +10%.
For spices, FDA import alerts (Salmonella, lead in ground cinnamon) decide more shipments than the tariff does.

faqs.question: Is coffee exempt from tariffs?
searchedAs: is coffee still exempt from tariffs
is coffee exempt from us tariffs
are coffee beans exempt from tariffs
is green coffee exempt from tariffs
faqs.answer: Yes, from every country except China. Coffee has a Free base rate, and every coffee line is on the U.S. note 52(b) exemption list (9903.05.86), so the 10%–12.5% Section 301 tariffs that started July 24, 2026 do not apply. Coffee from China pays 7.5% under Section 301 List 4A. The 2025 IEEPA tariffs, from which coffee was exempted on November 13, 2025, ended on February 24, 2026.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on coffee from Brazil?
searchedAs: is brazilian coffee exempt from tariffs
faqs.answer: Zero. Green and roasted coffee are Free, and Brazil's 25% Section 301 tariff (9903.05.01) and its 12.5% forced-labor tariff exempt coffee (9903.05.03, 9903.05.86). From August 6 to November 12, 2025 Brazilian coffee paid 50% (10% reciprocal plus 40% under Executive Order 14323); Executive Orders 14360 and 14361 removed both for coffee from November 13, 2025. The U.S. imported $2.52B of coffee from Brazil in 2025.

faqs.question: Are there tariffs on coffee from Colombia?
searchedAs: are there tariffs on coffee from colombia
what is the current tariff on coffee from colombia
faqs.answer: No. Coffee is Free, and Colombia's 12.5% Section 301 tariff (9903.05.32) does not apply to coffee (9903.05.86). The 10% reciprocal tariff of 2025 stopped applying to coffee on November 13, 2025 and ended on February 24, 2026. Colombia was the largest supplier of Chapter 09 goods in 2025, with $2.76B.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on coffee and pepper from Vietnam?
searchedAs: how to import coffee from vietnam
faqs.answer: None on coffee or black pepper: both are Free and exempt from Vietnam's 12.5% Section 301 tariff (9903.05.84). Dried chilies and paprika keep their 2.5¢–5¢/kg base rate. The 20% reciprocal rate on Vietnam ended on February 24, 2026. Vietnam supplied $1.11B of Chapter 09 goods in 2025, including 39% of U.S. pepper and capsicum imports.

faqs.question: What is the U.S. tariff on spices from India?
searchedAs: tariff on spices from india to usa
faqs.answer: Only the base rate, which is Free for black pepper, cumin, turmeric, cardamom and most other spices. India's 10% Section 301 tariff (9903.05.44) applies only to thyme and bay leaves (0910.99.05, 0910.99.06). The 2025 IEEPA duties on India — 25% reciprocal plus an additional 25% — ended in February 2026. Indian spices still need FDA prior notice, and Indian black pepper falls under FDA Import Alert 28-02, which requires an Export Inspection Council certificate for each lot.

faqs.question: Is there a tariff on matcha or tea from Japan?
searchedAs: is there a tariff on matcha
faqs.answer: Plain green tea and matcha (0902.10.90, 0902.20.90) are Free. Flavored green tea is 6.4%, or 3.2% with a Japan agreement claim. Japan's 12.5% Section 301 rate does not apply to tea (9903.05.86). Japan supplied $190M of tea in 2025, 31% of U.S. tea imports.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on tea and spices from China?
faqs.answer: The base rate plus 7.5%. Section 301 List 4A (9903.88.15) covers every Chapter 09 line from China, and USTR kept it in place on October 7, 2026. Plain tea is Free at base, so it pays 7.5%; flavored green tea pays 6.4% + 7.5% = 13.9%; thyme pays 4.8% + 20%. The 2025 IEEPA duties on China ended on February 24, 2026.

faqs.question: Is there a tariff on coffee from Canada?
faqs.answer: No. Coffee and tea are Free, and they are exempt from the 10% Section 301 tariff on Canadian goods whether or not they qualify for USMCA. No Chapter 09 line is on the 2026 Canada Section 338 lists. The 35% IEEPA duty on non-USMCA Canadian goods ended on February 24, 2026.

faqs.question: Is there a tariff on vanilla, cinnamon or black pepper?
searchedAs: is there a tariff on vanilla
is there a tariff on cinnamon
is there a tariff on black pepper
faqs.answer: Vanilla, cinnamon and black pepper are Free, whole or ground, and exempt from the 2026 Section 301 tariffs. Madagascar, which supplied 70% of U.S. vanilla imports in 2025, is not one of the 60 economies anyway. Only goods from China pay extra (+7.5%). Ground cinnamon from firms on FDA Import Alert 99-42 is detained for lead.

faqs.question: What is the HTS code for green coffee beans?
searchedAs: hts code for green coffee beans
hs code for green coffee beans
hs code green bean coffee arabica
hs code green bean coffee robusta
faqs.answer: Green (not roasted) coffee is 0901.11 if not decaffeinated and 0901.12 if decaffeinated. The 10-digit lines are split by type: 0901.11.00.15 (arabica, certified organic), 0901.11.00.25 (arabica, other), 0901.11.00.35 and .40 (robusta), 0901.11.00.50 and .65 (other). Roasted coffee is 0901.21 and 0901.22. All are Free.

faqs.question: What is the HTS code for tea and tea bags?
faqs.answer: Green tea is 0902.10 in packings of 3 kg or less and 0902.20 in larger packings; black and partly fermented (oolong) tea is 0902.30 in packings of 3 kg or less and 0902.40 otherwise. Black tea in tea bags is 0902.30.00.15 (organic) or 0902.30.00.50. Herbal infusions without tea leaves are not in Chapter 09.

faqs.question: What is the HTS code for spices and spice powders?
searchedAs: hs code for spices chili powder
faqs.answer: Each spice has its own heading, whole or ground: pepper and chili 0904, vanilla 0905, cinnamon 0906, cloves 0907, nutmeg and cardamom 0908, seeds such as cumin and coriander 0909, ginger, turmeric, curry and thyme 0910. Mixtures of spices from different headings are 0910.91 (1.9%). Mixed seasonings that lose the character of spices, such as many masalas with salt or other ingredients, go to heading 2103 (Chapter 09 note 1).

faqs.question: Do you need a license to import coffee into the U.S.?
searchedAs: do you need a license to import coffee
how to import coffee beans to usa
faqs.answer: No import license is needed. FDA requires prior notice of each shipment before arrival, a registered foreign facility (roaster, packer or warehouse) and a Foreign Supplier Verification Program kept by the U.S. importer. Organic coffee needs an NOP Import Certificate, and unroasted coffee may not be shipped into Hawaii or Puerto Rico.
